questions.q: A farmer in the Ganga-Yamuna Doab finds white calcareous nodules (kankar) at 1-2 metres depth in his field. The soil is clayey loam, light grey, and requires regular nitrogen fertiliser. Identify the soil type and its local name.
questions.a: The soil is Bangar (old alluvium). The presence of kankar (calcium carbonate nodules) at depth, light grey colour, clayey loam texture, and nitrogen deficiency are diagnostic features of Bangar. A wrong answer (e.g., identifying it as Khadar) reveals the student confuses the age sequence — Khadar lacks kankar, is darker, finer, and more fertile because it is annually renewed by floods.

questions.q: Explain why Khadar soils in the active floodplain of the Brahmaputra in Assam are more suitable for jute cultivation than Bangar soils on the higher terraces of the same region.
questions.a: Khadar soils receive annual fresh silt deposits during monsoon floods, maintaining high fertility, fine texture (silty clay), good moisture retention, and neutral pH — ideal for water-intensive jute. Bangar soils on higher terraces are above flood level, so they miss annual renewal; they develop kankar, become coarser, lose nitrogen through leaching, and require artificial irrigation and fertilisation. A wrong answer indicates the student does not link flood dynamics to soil renewal and fertility maintenance.

questions.q: Given a soil sample from a coastal delta with the following properties: pH 6.5, texture silty clay, organic carbon 0.8%, available nitrogen low, available phosphorus medium, available potassium high, no kankar. Classify it as Bangar or Khadar and justify using three diagnostic criteria.
questions.a: Step 1: Note the absence of kankar — rules out Bangar (kankar is diagnostic of old alluvium). Step 2: Silty clay texture and high potassium indicate recent deposition — characteristic of Khadar. Step 3: Low nitrogen despite high potassium matches Khadar's profile (nitrogen leaches quickly in new deposits; potassium persists from mineral weathering). Step 4: Coastal delta location confirms active floodplain setting. This is Khadar. A wrong classification shows inability to use multiple soil properties simultaneously for identification.

questions.q: Compare the agricultural land use patterns in the Bangar belt of the Punjab-Haryana plain versus the Khadar belt of the lower Ganga plain in West Bengal. Explain the role of soil age, texture, and water availability in creating these differences.
questions.a: Punjab-Haryana Bangar: Coarse texture, kankar layer impedes drainage, low organic matter → requires canal irrigation (Bhakra Nangal), heavy fertiliser (N, P), supports wheat-rice rotation with high inputs. West Bengal Khadar: Fine texture, annual silt renewal, high moisture retention, near-permanent water table → supports 2-3 crops/year (rice-jute-rice), lower fertiliser need. The difference arises because Bangar is an old, uplifted terrace away from active floods, while Khadar is actively flooded. A weak answer treats both as "alluvial" without distinguishing age-driven property changes.

questions.q: Evaluate the sustainability of current intensive rice-wheat cropping on Khadar soils of the Indo-Gangetic Plain considering soil health indicators: declining organic carbon, rising salinity in irrigated patches, and groundwater depletion.
questions.a: Current practice is unsustainable. Khadar's natural fertility renewal by floods is disrupted by embankments and dams (e.g., Farakka, Tehri). Rice-wheat rotation mines nitrogen and potassium; puddling for rice destroys soil structure; flood irrigation raises water table and brings salts up in semi-arid zones (e.g., southwestern Punjab). Organic carbon has dropped below 0.3% in many areas. Sustainable alternatives: conservation agriculture (zero-till, residue retention), crop diversification (pulses, maize), and managed aquifer recharge. An answer calling it "sustainable because Khadar is fertile" ignores the broken renewal cycle and input-driven yield maintenance.

questions.q: Design a soil survey transect across the Ganga floodplain from the active channel to the upland terrace to map the Bangar-Khadar transition. Specify sampling intervals, depth, and three key parameters to measure at each point.
questions.a: Transect: Perpendicular to river, 5 km total length. Sampling: Every 500 m (11 points). Depth: 0-15 cm (topsoil), 15-50 cm (subsoil), 50-100 cm (substratum). Parameters: (1) Texture (sand-silt-clay %) by hydrometer — expects fining toward channel; (2) Calcium carbonate (%) by HCl effusion — expects kankar peak in Bangar zone (2-4 km from channel); (3) Organic carbon (%) by Walkley-Black — expects higher in Khadar topsoil. Good answer includes spatial reasoning; poor answer samples randomly or omits depth-wise sampling missing the kankar horizon.
